newsitem.title: CHINA: Chinese exporters worry about yuan's steady rise.
newsitem.headline: Chinese exporters worry about yuan's steady rise.

text.p: Chinese exporters said on Wednesday they were concerned that the gradually strengthening yuan was squeezing their profit margins and could start to weaken their competitiveness on the world market.

They said the slow but relentless rise of the Chinese yuan against the U.S. dollar was threatening their already paper-thin profit margins, the result of internal inefficiencies and fierce competition between Chinese exporters.
The Chinese yuan has been steadily pushing upwards for over a year, and hit a two-year high of 8.2917 against the U.S. dollar on Tuesday, up from 8.2982 at the beginning of the year.

Most of China's state-owned import and export companies have been facing increasing problems over the past couple of years after their monopolies on exporting certain commodities were abandoned and the market thrown open to other firms.
China registered a trade surplus of $10.29 billion in the first four months of this year, a massive increase from $6.71 billion in the first three months, official figures showed.

"The substantial trade surplus does not mean solid profits," said a trader from one major Shanghai import and export company. "Many export companies have lowered their profit margins to very low levels, some are even suffering losses."

"Small exporting companies have mushroomed in the past few years," an exporter with a local state-owned import and export company said. "In order to get exporting contracts, they cut prices to low levels, which forces us to follow even though our products are better quality."
Exporters said such low profit margins made them very sensitive to foreign exchange rate changes even though the Chinese currency was among the most stable in the world.
The yuan rose just 0.3 percent in 1996 against the dollar and has risen a further 0.08 percent since the start of the year.
"We have not suffered losses from the recent steady gains in the local currency as the pace of the increase has been very slow," said a trader with one of Shanghai's largest exporting companies.
"But we worry about its further strong momentum, which will eat up our already low profits and erode our competitiveness."

"For every dollar of commodities being exported, we can earn only 0.06 to 0.07 yuan under the current exchange cost of 8.3 yuan, if the yuan advances to the 8.26 level, we will have no profit at all," a textile exporter said.

Foreign exchange dealers said the yuan was likely to soon test the key 8.2900 level against the U.S. dollar given the substantial trade surplus and reduced central bank intervention to depress the currency. The yuan ended Wednesday at 8.2924 against the dollar.
